name: Gohyakumangoku (sake rice of Niigata)
text: Sake-brewing rice bred at the Niigata Agricultural Experiment Station in 1938. It was named in 1957 to mark Niigata's rice crop reaching 5 million koku (about 750,000 t). It is the rice behind the clean, dry Niigata style and is also a mainstay in Toyama and Fukui; one Fukui-oriented source says Fukui ranks second nationally in Gohyakumangoku volume.
flavor: Clean, light, crisp; little aromatic ornament, dry finish.
use: Core rice for futsu-shu through ginjo in Niigata, Toyama and Fukui; chosen when the goal is a tight, quiet cup that sits behind food.
craft: Sources describe the grain as somewhat hard and slow to dissolve, so it is not suited to very high polishing; it takes koji well and absorbs water readily. Judge by how the moromi melts late and cleanly: it tends to give a thin, dry body rather than richness, so brewers use it where lightness is the aim rather than trying to force depth from it.

name: Koshitanrei (Niigata ginjo rice, Niigata Sake No. 72)
text: Niigata's own ginjo rice, Yamada-nishiki x Gohyakumangoku (mother Yamada-nishiki, father Gohyakumangoku), developed under an 'All Niigata' concept so that rice, water and skill all come from the prefecture. It is a late cultivar, heading and ripening about 15 days after Gohyakumangoku. The name joins 'Koshi' (Niigata) with 'tanrei'. Registration date is given inconsistently: a prefectural research page lists registration no. 15536 on 7 Aug 2007, while another article says 2004.
flavor: Fine, soft, clean; the idea is an elegant tanrei profile in the daiginjo range.
use: Junmai ginjo to junmai daiginjo from Niigata kura; sold as a regional-pride rice.
craft: Large grain with low brown-rice protein, said to withstand polishing to 40 percent or less, which is why it targets daiginjo. Check protein and grain size per harvest; because it heads late, harvest timing and field weather swing quality more than with early Gohyakumangoku.

name: Echigo toji (Niigata brewing guild)
text: One of Japan's major toji (master brewer) groups, born in Niigata. It originated in the Edo period when farmers idle under heavy snow went to breweries for winter work, and grew after the 1754 'katte-zukuri' deregulation shifted brewing toward winter kan-zukuri. The modern organization was formed in 1958 and sits under a prefectural federation of brewery employees. The Kariwa-gun area is cited as the origin of the guild. Sources divide the sub-schools differently, as three (Mishima, Kariwa, Kubiki) or four with Koshiji and Notsumi added.
flavor: The Niigata ideal: clean, lean and smooth rather than heavy.
use: Understanding who runs the kura: many Niigata breweries are traditionally staffed by Echigo toji and kurabito.
craft: Training now runs through the Niigata Sake School, founded in 1984 in Niigata City for successor development. Figures for membership vary by source and year, so confirm with the federation before quoting numbers.
src: Niigata Bunka Monogatari: Echigo toji and brewing songs
Sake Times: the three great toji groups

name: Yukimuro and snow-storage aging (Niigata)
text: Niigata kura store sake in snow rooms or snow-covered stores, using the stable low temperature of the snowpack. Reported conditions vary: Hakkaisan says its yukimuro holds about 3 degrees C, one Echigo store cites about 2 degrees C and 90 percent humidity, and Takanoi (Ojiya) describes 0 degrees C and 100 percent humidity inside the snow. Tamagawa Shuzo says snow-aging research began in the 1980s and its oldest surviving bottle dates from 1985.
flavor: Rounded, softened, mellow; sharp edges are said to be reduced.
use: Aged junmai ginjo and daiginjo, served chilled; limited volumes because the snow rooms are small.
craft: Hakkaisan brews special sake for its 3-year and 8-year yukimuro releases rather than using its regular products, which signals that base-sake design matters. The claim that snow aging gives mellowness is the makers' description, not a measured result; judge by tasting against the same sake held conventionally.
src: Echigo Yukikura long snow storage daiginjo
UX Niigata TV21: Takanoi snow storage

name: Oyamanishiki (Toyama sake rice)
text: Toyama Prefecture's sake rice, bred at the Toyama Agricultural Technology Center: crossed in 1986 from Hidahomare (mother) and Akita Sake 33 (father), given the local number 'Toyama Sake 45', named Oyamanishiki in October 1998 and adopted as a recommended sake rice in July 1999. Aim was an early-maturing, high-shinpaku rice, since Gohyakumangoku lodges and is hard to polish for ginjo. It matures a few days after Gohyakumangoku, is slightly taller but lodging-resistant and high yielding.
flavor: Clean and moderately full, with a fine structure at high polish.
use: Junmai ginjo and daiginjo from Toyama; 100 percent Toyama-grown bottlings are sold as an all-Toyama product.
craft: Large thousand-grain weight and good shinpaku favor koji growth; absorbs water fast and resists breaking at high polish, so soaking must be watched closely by the second. Registration dates differ across sources (the 1986 cross to 1998 naming and a later registration), so cite the naming year when quoting.
src: JA Zen-Noh Toyama: all-Toyama junmai ginjo Oyama

name: Toyama sake: Tateyama meltwater and Etchu style
ja: 富山の酒（立山の伏流水）
text: Toyama sake is tied to snowmelt from the Tateyama range and the sub-surface flow of rivers such as the Joganji and Sho. Trade guides say many breweries use soft water from this source and local rice such as Oyamanishiki, Gohyakumangoku and Yamada-nishiki. Style is not uniform: some sources call it tanrei-karakuchi, others mellow and flavorful. Claims of national rankings for named waters come mainly from commercial articles and were not backed by official statistics in the results.
flavor: Soft water gives a gentle, round texture; character varies by kura from crisp to mellow.
use: Chosen as a clean, water-led sake for meals; style differs by kura, so taste the specific bottling before pairing.
craft: Soft water ferments fast and tends to be mild on mineral backbone, so check acidity and ageing potential rather than assuming structure. Treat the water-ranking and rice-share claims as unverified until confirmed with the Toyama brewers' association.

name: Hyakumangoku-no-shiro (Ishikawa sake rice, Ishikawa Sake No. 68)
text: Ishikawa's own daiginjo rice, developed by the Ishikawa Agriculture and Forestry Research Center over about 11 years from 2005 at breweries' request for a prefectural rice for daiginjo; the earlier Ishikawa-mon (2009) targeted ginjo, while daiginjo mostly used Yamada-nishiki. Releases began in April 2020. Lineage is described variously: one shop describes a cross of Hitohana and Koshitanrei with Yamada-nishiki, while others only give the code 'Ishikawa Sake 68'.
flavor: Light yet substantial; low protein gives a clean, smooth mouthfeel.
use: Daiginjo and junmai ginjo from Ishikawa kura, sold as an Ishikawa-grown daiginjo.
craft: Sources say it resists cracking at high polish and has a small shinpaku, tolerating polishing past 50 percent. One account also calls the grain small, hard and slow to absorb water, so soaking time and steaming should be set by trial. Maker experience is still accumulating.
src: Honno Hitotoki: Ishikawa original sake rice

name: Kaga no Kikuzake and Kikuhime yamahai junmai
ja: 加賀の菊酒・菊姫 山廃純米
text: 'Kaga no kikuzake' is a late-Muromachi sake from Kaga said in documents to have been sent to Kyoto. Kikuhime (Hakusan) uses Tedori River water from Mt Hakusan, and its name comes from Kukurihime, deity of the Shirayama shrine. Makers' accounts say it sold the first junmai labelled yamahai in 1978 under toji Noguchi Naohiko, with a yamahai ginjo the next year. Its yamahai junmai uses Yamada-nishiki from the Tokku-A zone of Yoshikawa, Miki, at 70 percent polish.
flavor: Rich, full, strongly rice-driven with firm acidity.
use: Sipped at room temperature or warmed; suited to strong flavors such as simmered dishes and cured fish.
craft: Yamahai means skipping the pole-ramming (yamaoroshi) step, which lengthens and complicates acid development; the style needs a seasoned toji. Founding-year and Muromachi claims are from the makers' profiles and not independently confirmed in these results.

name: Sakahomare (Fukui daiginjo rice)
text: Fukui's new sake rice, developed from 2010 by the prefectural agricultural station together with the Fukui Sake Brewers' Association, aimed at daiginjo; the name carries the wish for 'Japan's best sake'. Reported to be polishable to 35 percent. It is grown under the prefecture's special cultivation certification, with chemical pesticides and fertilizer cut by at least half and organic fertilizer used. Seventeen Fukui kura released daiginjo from it on a single national date, 19 April.
flavor: Refined sweetness and aroma at high polish.
use: Daiginjo, usually with prefecture-bred Fukui yeast; the 17-brewery release was sold as a group launch.
craft: Paired with Fukui yeasts FK-501 (clean), FK-801C and FK-802 (aromatic). Verify the polishing ratio and brown-rice quality per lot since the rice is new and grown under reduced-chemical rules.
src: Sake Times: 17 Fukui kura Sakahomare daiginjo

name: Kuzuryu rice (Fukui revived sake rice)
text: Kuzuryu is a rare Fukui sake-rice variety revived after about ten years of absence, used by Tanabe Shuzo in its 'Echizen Misaki' revived-rice junmai. At Nibu Shuzo in Echizen, the toji grows Kuzuryu himself and brews it by kimoto in the 'Asukai' line; another maker uses Eiheiji-grown Kuzuryu at 100 percent. The rice name is not the same as the 'Kuzuryu' brand from Kokuryu Shuzo (founded 1804), which is a second label.
flavor: Not detailed in sources; sold as a restrained junmai style.
use: Junmai, often kimoto, as a Fukui local-rice story.
craft: Cultivar characteristics such as aroma and polishing behavior were not found in the results, so evaluate lot by lot. Do not confuse the rice (Kuzuryu) with the Kokuryu brand (Kuzuryu).

name: Fukui FK yeasts (FK-501, FK-801C, FK-802)
text: Fukui Prefecture has its own FK-series sake yeasts. FK-501 is described as giving a clean, crisp style, while FK-801C and FK-802 are described as giving a showy aroma. Breweries use them with Fukui rice: Obama Shuzo ferments daiginjo with FK-801C at long low temperature, Tanabe Shuzo uses FK801 with Koshi-no-shizuku, and Nibu Shuzo uses FK801 with Sakahomare. Notation (FK-801, FK801, FK-801C) varies by seller, and the results do not say whether they are the same strain.
flavor: FK-501 clean; FK-801C and FK-802 fragrant.
use: Choose by target: FK-501 for light food-friendly sake, FK-801C or FK-802 for aromatic ginjo and daiginjo.
craft: Confirm the exact strain code with the supplier before specifying a recipe, and do not assume FK-801 and FK-801C behave identically.

name: Shichiken (Hakushu, Yamanashi) and Kaikoma meltwater
text: Yamanashi Meijo in Hakushu-cho, Hokuto is credited with a founding in 1750 (Kankyo 3), and sits at the foot of Mt Kaikoma, inside the Minami Alps Biosphere Reserve (certified 2014). Its brewing water is Kaikoma sub-surface flow, which the brewery presents as about 85 percent of the product. It says it uses 95 percent or more local rice from contract farms. The flagship is junmai daiginjo 'Kinu no Aji', and it makes a bottle-fermented sparkling 'Shichiken Sparkling'. Hokuto city and the prefecture list Daikan, Shun-o-ten and Shichiken as the South Alps water breweries.
flavor: Soft, gentle and rounded; the brewery stresses a calm, comfortable drinking character.
use: Table sake; the sparkling is an aperitif.
craft: Soft mountain water suits slow, careful fermentation; judge softness, not weight. Figures for water share and local rice are the brewery's own statements.
src: Yamanashi Tourism: South Alps meltwater sake
Hokuto City: Mizu no Yama column

name: Miyamanishiki (Nagano cold-region sake rice)
text: Bred at Nagano's agricultural experiment station by selecting a radiation-induced mutant of Takane-nishiki. By 2022 it was third in national sake-rice production after Yamada-nishiki and Gohyakumangoku. It tolerates cold, so it is grown in cold regions as well as Nagano. Brews are described as modest in aroma, with little off-note and a tanrei style.
flavor: Light, crisp, clean; restrained aroma.
use: Junmai, honjozo and ginjo across the cold north; the standard rice for Nagano's clear style.
craft: A stable, cold-tolerant cultivar, so supply is reliable. Because aroma is modest, yeast choice drives the character in ginjo.

name: Hitogokochi (Nagano sake rice)
text: Nagano-born sake rice, larger than Miyamanishiki and with good shinpaku expression. It is cold tolerant and resists lodging in wind, so it is easy to grow. The sake is described as clean tanrei with some range. The large shinpaku also means it is not well suited to heavy polishing.
flavor: Crisp, light, with breadth in flavor.
use: Junmai and junmai ginjo at moderate polish.
craft: Large shinpaku means a strong koji growth but a risk of breaking when polished hard; match polish ratio to the grain rather than chasing daiginjo numbers.

name: Kinmon-nishiki (Nagano 'phantom' sake rice)
text: A cross of Takane-nishiki and Yamada-nishiki, known as a 'phantom rice' in Nagano. Described as having complex umami and aroma, flavor that opens with time and suitability for aging, used in premium junmai daiginjo. One source says it is grown only in Kijimadaira Village, while another says it is now grown in various places in the prefecture.
flavor: Complex, deep umami with aroma; ages well.
use: Premium junmai ginjo and daiginjo; candidates for aging.
craft: Described as difficult to grow and to brew; quantities are small, so lock in supply early.

name: Nagano's seven approved sake-rice cultivars
ja: 長野県の産地品種銘柄（酒米7品種）
text: Nagano permits the origin-and-cultivar label for seven sake rices: Takane-nishiki, Kinmon-nishiki, Shirakaba-nishiki, Hitogokochi, Miyamanishiki, Yamae-nishiki and Yamada-nishiki. Nagano's brewers' association counted 80 kura as of 19 Aug 2025, second in Japan, while GI Nagano says 78 and a 2018 tax survey says 75, so the count depends on date and source.
flavor: Range from clean Miyamanishiki to deep Kinmon-nishiki.
use: Labeling and sourcing: a regional-rice list used to specify provenance on a menu or in purchasing.
craft: The list is reported secondhand; confirm the current official list with the Nagano brewers' association. Note the rice name 'Shirakaba-nishiki' and 'Yamae-nishiki' are less documented here.

name: Alps yeast (Nagano C yeast)
ja: アルプス酵母（長野C酵母）
text: A yeast developed by the Nagano food industry test station, now called Nagano C yeast. It produces a lot of apple-like aroma, cited as one reason Nagano sake is called fruity. It sits alongside the Kyokai No. 7 yeast, which originated at Miyasaka Brewing in Suwa.
flavor: Apple-like fruity aroma.
use: Ginjo and junmai ginjo with a fruity profile.
craft: Aroma is yeast-driven; watch fermentation temperature to keep it from tipping into solvent notes.

name: Hidahomare (Gifu sake rice)
text: A Gifu original sake rice bred in 1972 at the Gifu Highland Agricultural Experiment Station. Grains are large with a very high shinpaku rate and low protein. It is also the mother of Toyama's Oyamanishiki. Local brewers say balance and ease of drinking are its strengths.
flavor: Balanced, easy-drinking, with little coarseness.
use: Junmai ginjo and ginjo-type styles from Hida and Gifu.
craft: High water absorption and solubility suit junmai ginjo; adjust steeping to avoid over-melting.

name: Gifu G yeast series (G, G2, NFG)
text: Gifu's own yeast series. The name is tied to the Gifu brewers' quality-guarantee G mark (GOOD, GOLD, GIFU). A foam-free version called NFG was developed and is used in commercial sake. G2 was designed to raise ethyl caproate to more than three times the base G yeast; sales to 15 Gifu breweries started in fiscal 2018. NFG is restricted to Gifu businesses; in Feb 2026 a Mizunami craft brewery issued the first beer using it.
flavor: G2 emphasizes fruity ethyl caproate aroma.
use: Aromatic ginjo and junmai ginjo from Gifu breweries.
craft: The foam-free strain reduces tank overflow and eases volume management at high filling.
src: PR Times: NFG yeast craft beer

name: Shizuoka yeast (HD-1 and NEW-5)
text: Shizuoka's prefectural yeasts, said to be used by over 80 percent of the prefecture's makers. HD-1 was isolated in 1978 by Kawamura Denbei from day-13 moromi at Kaiun's daiginjo kura; it gives a high ginjo aroma with somewhat higher acidity and is said to have driven Shizuoka's mass awards at the 1986 national new sake appraisal. NEW-5 is a hybrid with HD-1 as a parent: lighter, softer aroma and acidity about 0.2 lower.
flavor: HD-1: melon-like ginjo aroma and firm acid; NEW-5: lighter, low-acid, clean.
use: HD-1 for ginjo and daiginjo; NEW-5 for junmai ginjo that pairs well with food.
craft: Choose NEW-5 when you need lower acidity without losing a soft fragrance; HD-1 when you want a stronger aromatic and acid frame.

name: Homarefuji (Shizuoka sake rice)
text: Shizuoka's first original sake rice, bred at the Shizuoka Agriculture and Forestry Research Institute by gamma-irradiating Yamada-nishiki seed from 1998 and selecting a mutant. Variety registration was approved in March 2009. Sources differ on the number of seeds or individuals screened (100,000 vs 98,000). It is shorter than Yamada-nishiki and resists lodging, with a larger shinpaku that tolerates high polish.
flavor: Fruity top aroma, fresh and light.
use: Junmai ginjo and ginjo; the 'all-Shizuoka' formula pairs it with Shizuoka yeast and local water.
craft: Easier to grow than Yamada-nishiki; the large shinpaku helps koji growth, but verify polishing yield per lot.

name: Wakamizu (Aichi sake rice)
text: Sake rice developed in Aichi, adopted as a recommended variety in 1983 per one source (another says the 1980s). It is described as high in umami, suited to non-cold regions, large grained and easily dissolved in the moromi. It is easy to grow on flat ground with short culms. Compared with Yamada-nishiki it is hard to polish and breaks if polished too far.
flavor: Umami-rich, full.
use: Junmai and honjozo with body; not for daiginjo-level polish.
craft: Cap the polish ratio; dissolves readily so control temperature and koji to avoid heavy, sticky finishes.

name: Yumeginga (Aichi sake rice)
text: A cross of Yamada-nishiki and Wakamizu developed by the Aichi Agricultural Research Center. Its shinpaku is smaller than Wakamizu's, so it can be polished higher, and its brewing suitability is rated on par with Yamada-nishiki. It resists leaf-stripe disease and suits flat ground, notably the Chita Peninsula and West Mikawa. Dates conflict: one source says developed in 2010, another says crossed in 2001 and registered in 2012.
flavor: Fresh with umami.
use: Junmai ginjo and regional all-Aichi releases.
craft: Higher polish than Wakamizu is feasible; confirm the heading date for your field.

name: Kami-no-ho (Mie sake rice)
text: A Mie original sake rice, developed in 2007 and registered in 2010 at the request of breweries. A toji describes its character as 'clean aroma and swelling flavor'. It takes up water slowly, which makes brewing difficult. It is commonly paired with Mie's MK yeasts, and used in junmai ginjo and daiginjo.
flavor: Clean aroma with a rounded, expanding taste.
use: Junmai ginjo and daiginjo from Mie kura.
craft: Slow water absorption demands precise soaking and steaming; judge by feel and weight.
src: Bungo no Bonjovi: Mie MK yeast and Kami-no-ho

name: Ise-nishiki (Mie heritage sake rice)
text: A landrace-type rice found in Taki, Mie, called one of Japan's oldest sake-rice lines and linked to Yamada-nishiki's ancestry. It lapsed for a time. It is now grown at only about 15 t a year. An older Mie University-linked description says sake from it is lighter and more refreshing than from Yamada-nishiki, but this comes from an old website.
flavor: Light, refreshing.
use: Rare junmai ginjo releases.
craft: Very small volume means high cost and little buffer; secure contracts early.

name: Mie MK yeasts (MK1, MK3, MK5, MK7)
text: Yeasts developed by the Mie Prefecture Industrial Research Institute and distributed to makers. The institute describes MK1 as suited to junmai and ginjo with low acid; MK3 as ginjo-type with strong ethyl caproate; MK5 as junmai-type rich in succinic acid. In a comparison study MK1 gave more isoamyl acetate than Kyokai yeasts and MK3 higher alcohol and aroma. MK7 was designed for a high-acid, wine-like sake.
flavor: MK1 mild; MK3 apple-fruity; MK5 full; MK7 sharply acidic.
use: Select by target profile; MK3 with Kami-no-ho is a common junmai daiginjo pairing.
craft: Read the supplier sheet for the strain's acid and ester profile and dial fermentation temperature accordingly.
src: Comparison of components of Mie yeast sake

name: Shiga Watarifune No. 6
text: A heritage sake rice from Shiga, said to have been bred in 1916 at the Shiga Agricultural Experiment Station by pure-line selection from the older Watarifune. A blog notes that No. 6 was the easier to grow of the Watarifune lines, so seed remained at the station. Culm-length records disagree between Hyogo and Fukui trials, and relation to the 'short-culm Watarifune' (father of Yamada-nishiki) is debated. Makers describe rich rice umami and sweetness; it is lodging-prone and hard to grow.
flavor: Rich umami and sweetness, rounded.
use: Yamahai and junmai bottled as heritage-rice sake.
craft: Lodging risk means yield and rice quality swing by year; the yamahai pairing is common.

name: Ginfubuki (Shiga sake rice)
text: A Shiga sake rice with Yamada-nishiki as mother and Tamasakae as father, developed mainly to improve Yamada-nishiki's tall, lodging-prone growth. It is used in Maibara for the local 'Hananoibuki' with Ibuki mountain water, described as mellow with a crisp finish.
flavor: Mellow rice umami with a crisp finish.
use: Junmai ginjo and local-ingredient releases.
craft: Easier to grow than Yamada-nishiki; judge culm height and lodging.

name: Omi sake: lakeside breweries of Shiga
text: Shiga's brewing grew along the Tokaido and Nakasendo crossroads and the Lake Biwa water routes, with Omi merchants carrying trade east. Notable old houses include Tomita Shuzo (1534, called the fifth oldest sake company), Fujii Honke (1831), Kita Shuzo (1820) and Uehara Shuzo (1862). Tomita uses Okuibuki sub-surface water, Kitajima Shuzo uses Suzuka range water. Dates vary by page.
flavor: Varies by kura; soft mountain water supports gentle, rounded sake.
use: Regional pairing with lake fish such as funa-zushi.
craft: Check each house's water source and rice; a single 'Omi style' does not exist.

name: Iwai (Kyoto original sake rice)
text: Kyoto's own sake rice, born in 1933 at the Tango branch of the Kyoto Prefectural Agricultural Experiment Station and grown on over 600 ha by 1936. It faded in postwar food-increase policy (JA says it stopped in 1973 because tall straw did not suit machine harvest). The Fushimi Sake Brewers' Association revived it from 1992 (Heisei 4) with farmers, and it was certified as a Kyoto brand product in fiscal 2012. Only Kyoto breweries use it.
flavor: Fine-grained, soft and full.
use: Ginjo and daiginjo; Saito Shuzo makes a junmai daiginjo polished to 35 percent.
craft: Tall plants and low yield limit supply; confirm cultivar supply and polish target.
src: JA Kyoto: Iwai and Kyo no Sake

name: Kyoto yeasts (Kyo no Koto, Hana, Saki, Haku, Koi)
text: Five yeasts developed by the Kyoto Municipal Institute of Industrial Technology and Culture, which has developed, managed and distributed sake yeast since the 1950s-60s. Distribution is limited to Kyoto breweries. Kyo no Saki is rich in malic acid with muscat aroma; Kyo no Haku makes extra succinic acid for warmed (kan) sake; Kyo no Koi (distributed since 2020, parent Kyo no Koto) gives a fruity, sweet-sour profile.
flavor: Saki: muscat and crisp; Haku: umami for warmed sake; Koi: fruity.
use: Specify Haku for jo-kan service; Saki and Koi for chilled sake.
craft: Properties of Kyo no Koto and Kyo no Hana were not found in the results; check with the institute.
src: Sake World: Kyoto yeast lab visit
Sake Times: Kyoto yeast sake set

name: Ikeda-zake and the Hokusetsu breweries (Osaka)
text: Ikeda and Itami sake were shipped in quantity to Edo in the early Edo period, ahead of Nada and Fushimi. One source says Ikeda had 33 breweries at its mid-Edo peak. Today Osaka's association lists about 12 kura across Hokusetsu (Nose, Ikeda, Takatsuki, Ibaraki), Kawachi and Senshu; examples are Kure-haru, Kotobuki-sakazuki, Kuninocho, Naniwa Masamune and Sen no Rikyu. Founding years conflict (Kure-haru 1701 vs 1751).
flavor: Varies by kura.
use: Context for sourcing Osaka sake.
craft: Use association pages for current kura lists.

name: Akishika (Nose, Osaka) own-field yamahai
text: Akishika Shuzo in Nose is said to have been founded in 1886 and brews only junmai. Its own rice fields grew from 3 a to 13 ha, farmed pesticide-free in a circular system reusing rice bran, hulls and sake lees. It sells yamahai junmai from its own-field Yamada-nishiki, including a 70 percent polish fire-treated bottling and a draw-straight namagenshu.
flavor: Fresh with a soft lactic acidity and concentrated rice flavor; green apple on the unpasteurized version.
use: Food sake; the shop pages recommend it with meals.
craft: Estate rice, yamahai acid and a junmai-only policy are the identifiers. Specs come from retail pages and vary.

name: Yamada-nishiki (Hyogo, king of sake rice)
text: Born in 1936 at the Hyogo Prefectural Agricultural Experiment Station from a cross of Yamada-ho (also written Yamada-no-tane in some sources) and Tanga-watarifune. February 2026 marked its 90th anniversary. Miki city is cited as the country's top producer, with production concentrated in North Harima and the Hanshin area.
flavor: Full, elegant, fine aromatic structure.
use: Daiginjo, junmai daiginjo and top-grade sake across Japan.
craft: Tall, lodging-prone; quality depends on zone, so ask for district.

name: Tokku-A district Yamada-nishiki (Yokawa, Tojo, Yashiro)
text: The top-grade Yamada-nishiki zone lies north of the Rokko range, in Miki and Kato. Sources vary on the exact list: some name Yokawa, Tojo and Yashiro as 'Tokku-A a', others Yokawa, Kuchi-Yokawa, Tojo and eastern Yashiro. Yokawa is said to be the origin of the village-rice system with Nada kura. Large day-night temperature differences and clay soil are cited, giving large, plump grain with good shinpaku.
flavor: Large, plump grain; full-bodied sake.
use: Premium sake-rice specification.
craft: Zone boundaries vary by source; verify against the JA grading sheet.

name: Hyogo-Kitanishiki (Hyogo sake rice)
text: A Hyogo sake rice from Nadahikari and Gohyakumangoku (parental roles not specified in the source), suited to Tajima and Tamba. The prefecture says it has large grain, good shinpaku and high brewing suitability, and strong lodging resistance.
flavor: Not described in the source.
use: Junmai and ginjo from northern Hyogo.
craft: Strong lodging resistance suits the cooler north.

name: Hyogo-Yumenishiki (Hyogo sake rice)
text: A Hyogo sake rice from the F2 of Kikuei x Yamada-nishiki and Hyogo line 23, targeted for West Harima. The prefecture states it has large grain, good shinpaku and high brewing suitability.
flavor: Not described in the source.
use: Junmai and ginjo from West Harima.
craft: Little published data, so confirm lot specs.

name: Tamba toji (Hyogo guild)
text: A brewing guild from the Tamba-Sasayama basin, Hyogo. The oldest record, per Sasayama city, is Shoemon of Hioki who served as toji for Yamatoya Honten in the Ikeda district, brewing 'Yamajirushi' and 'Taki no Mizu'. Origin dates vary among 1705, 1755 and 1775. Peak registration is cited as 5,000 people. After the mid-Edo period Tamba toji also worked in Ikeda, Itami, Nada and Imazu.
flavor: Associated with Nada's firm style.
use: Context for who has staffed Nada and Ikeda kura.
craft: Toji organizations are cooperatives handling employment and succession.

name: Tajima toji (northern Hyogo guild)
text: One of Japan's four great toji groups from Mikata-gun (Kami and Shinonsen) in snowy northern Hyogo. Its predecessor, the Mikata-gun Brewing Association, was founded 1 Oct 1911. Toji enter the kura after harvest in October and live in until March, six to seven months. It was 240 toji in 1989; in 2025 the prayer ceremony covered 29 toji and 52 kurabito, and a 2024 report counted 53 members working in 2 urban prefectures and 10 prefectures.
flavor: Known for adapting to every method.
use: Context for northern Hyogo and out-of-region kura staffing.
craft: 'One kura, one toji': each toji's style differs. Membership figures vary by year.

name: Itami morohaku (Itami clear sake)
text: Itami in Hyogo claims to be the birthplace of seishu on the strength of a Konoike shrine stele recording that in 1600 (Keicho 5) Yamanaka Shinroku Yukimoto first brewed clear sake; the lineage with Yamanaka Shikanosuke is tradition. 'Morohaku' means polished rice for both koji and kake-mai. Itami's chushaku shochu addition is cited as an origin of alcohol addition. The Nara temple origin of clear sake is acknowledged. Itami morohaku and Nada kiippon was recognized as Japan Heritage in 2020.
flavor: Historic: clear, high-class sake.
use: Historical context for Edo kudari-zake.
craft: Dates and lineage rest on a stele and local tradition.
src: Japan Heritage: Itami morohaku and Nada kiippon

name: Bodaimoto (Shoryakuji, Nara)
text: Called Japan's oldest sake starter, recorded in the Muromachi 'Goshu no Nikki' as Bodaisen, from Bodaisenji (Shoryakuji) in Nara. A lactic-acid soaking water (soyashi-mizu) is made first, then steamed rice and koji are added. Today the soyashi-mizu uses lactic acid bacteria found in the temple's rock-spring water. The research group formed in 1986 per Wikipedia (1996 per another site); bacterial discovery dates 1998 vs 1999. The starter is made in January at the Bodaimoto Seishu Festival.
flavor: Distinct lactic acidity.
use: Sake from member Nara kura.
craft: The soyashi-mizu step distinguishes it from kimoto; follow temperature records rigorously.
src: Nara City Tourism: Nara shrines and sake

name: Nanto morohaku (Nara temple sake)
text: Sake brewed in Nara's temples (soboshu) from the Muromachi period, especially at Bodaisenji (Shoryakuji). In the Azuchi-Momoyama period morohaku methods with polished rice emerged as Nanto morohaku. The Tamon-in Nikki (1478-1618) mentions Shoryakuji brewing, multi-step addition, morohaku and pasteurization. After clerical power was suppressed, the technology spread to other brewers and toji.
flavor: Historic.
use: Historical context.
craft: Dating depends on historical documents.

name: Wakayama: Heiwa Shuzo (Kid) and Nate Shuzo (Kuroushi)
ja: 和歌山の蔵（平和酒造・名手酒造店）
text: Heiwa Shuzo (Kainan) was founded in 1928 and named in memory of regaining its permit to brew after the war; its 'Kid' brand dates from 2007 and a profile says the brewers average in their 30s and Kid won gold at the IWC. Nate Shuzo (Kainan) makes 'Kuroushi' using filtered well water; one profile says over 95 percent of shipments are junmai ginjo.
flavor: Kid: modern and fruity; Kuroushi: mellow with depth.
use: Wakayama sake with fresh and contemporary styles.
craft: Claims are from tourism and lifestyle media; confirm specs with kura.

name: Kimoto (kimoto-zukuri, traditional starter)
text: Traditional sake starter method relying on natural lactic acid bacteria, including the pole-ramming step (yamaoroshi) in which steamed rice and koji are ground. The lactic acid created suppresses bad microbes. It is slower than sokujo and generally yields fuller, richer sake.
flavor: Rich, deep, savory.
use: Specification for rich sake suited to warming.
craft: Duration quoted as about 20 days to a month in various sources; note differences across sources.

name: Yamahai (yamahai-moto)
text: Starter derived from kimoto by abolishing the yamaoroshi pole-ramming step (the name abbreviates yamaoroshi haishi). One source dates its development to 1909 (Meiji 42). Lactic acid is still cultured naturally rather than added. Reported time is about 3-4 weeks.
flavor: Rich, tangy lactic acid.
use: Wide-bodied sake.
craft: Dates and durations vary across sources.

name: Sokujo-moto (quick starter)
text: Starter made by adding brewing lactic acid, developed in 1910 (Meiji 43) at the National Brewing Research Institute. It is the current mainstream; one source says about nine-tenths of sake is made this way. It takes about 10 days to two weeks, resulting in a lighter, cleaner profile than kimoto or yamahai.
flavor: Clean, light.
use: Everyday through premium sake.
craft: Added lactic acid makes the starter safe and quick.

name: Nigori-zake (cloudy sake)
text: Sake from moromi pressed through a coarse cloth or net so that much lees stays. Under tax law it counts as seishu because it has been pressed once; doburoku is unfiltered and classed as 'other brewed alcohol'. 'Katsusei nigori' is bottled unpasteurized, continues fermenting and has fizz.
flavor: Creamy, rice-sweet.
use: Dessert or spicy food pairing; shake gently.
craft: No standard mesh size; unpasteurized active bottles are pressure-hazardous.

name: Koshu (aged sake)
text: No legal definition. The Choki Jukusei-shu Kenkyukai's guide is sake aged at least 3 years at the brewery. Color moves from pale yellow toward amber and brown, and aromas of caramel, honey, dried fruit, nuts and spice develop.
flavor: Caramel, honey, nuts.
use: After-dinner or with rich foods.
craft: Color and age thresholds are reference points.
src: Sake World: aged sake research group

name: Awa sake (sparkling sake)
ja: awa酒（スパークリング日本酒）
text: Awa Sake Association was formed in 2016 to promote sparkling sake. Its criteria: rice, koji and water only, CO2 only from natural fermentation, clear appearance with a stream of bubbles when opened, at least 10 percent alcohol and at least 3.5 bar at 20 degrees C. Most use bottle secondary fermentation; tank is also allowed.
flavor: Light, fizzy, aperitif style.
use: Toast or aperitif.
craft: High pressure bottles may burst if stored warm.
